query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an advanced free‐energy based sampling framework that couples multi‐phase thermodynamic models with microstructure evolution simulations enables systematic control over phase transformations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, leading to tailored microstructures and improved mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA exhibiting a mixed-phase microstructure (e.g., FCC, B2, and possibly A2 phases) typical of conventionally processed samples.
generation.intervention: Application of a tailored heat treatment (or HPHT-like processing) protocol designed using a free‐energy sampling framework that maps the thermodynamic stability and kinetic pathways of multiple phases across a range of temperatures, times, and pressures.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled thermal profiles and possibly pressure conditions that are selected based on predictions from integrated thermodynamic and kinetic simulations.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase fractions and domain sizes of the evolving microstructure (e.g., relative amounts of ordered B2 and disordered FCC phases) that mediate the mechanical response.
generation.mechanism: By predicting the free-energy landscape of multiple competing phases through computational sampling, the method identifies processing windows that lower the thermodynamic driving forces for unwanted transformations while kinetically promoting desirable phase precipitation, thus reducing reliance on trial-and-error experiments.
generation.predicted_outcome: A more predictable and optimized phase evolution with a targeted balance of phases – leading to improved strength and ductility – compared to standard processing methods.
generation.baseline: Conventional heat treatment or processing routes based on empirical trial-and-error methods without predictive free-energy modeling.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness may be limited under extremely non-equilibrium conditions or when the alloy composition deviates significantly from the studied system; the approach assumes availability of accurate thermodynamic databases.
generation.uncertainty: While simulations indicate potential improvements in phase control, the precise magnitude of mechanical property enhancements and the full applicability across varied processing regimes remain to be experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples: one set processed via conventional heat treatment (control) and another set processed using a heat treatment schedule optimized by the free‐energy sampling framework. Characterize the phase fractions and microstructure (using XRD, SEM, and TEM) and evaluate mechanical properties (e.g., hardness, tensile/compressive tests).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed using the simulation-guided heat treatment do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in phase control (i.e., closer to targeted phase fractions) and corresponding mechanical property enhancement relative to the conventionally processed samples, the hypothesis that the free‐energy sampling framework enables systematic control over phase evolution will be falsified.

Discovering novel high entropy alloys (HEAs) with exceptional performance has ushered in a new era for materials design [1] – [3] . The melting temperature is a crucial parameter in the search for such materials. For instance, a correlation between a high melting point and elevated temperature strength has been identified in refractory complex concentrated alloys [4] . Besides the melting temperature, other melting properties, such as enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, are also crucial for constructing phase diagrams and developing novel materials. However, experimental measurements on these properties, even for unary refractory materials, face severe challenges due to high melting points, often resulting in very scattered experimental data, if available at all. Additionally, the vast compositional space of HEAs makes systematic experimental screening of promising candidates impractical.

Materials performance is central to the satisfactory operation of current and future nuclear energy systems due to the severe irradiation environment in reactors. Searching for structural materials with excellent irradiation tolerance is crucial for developing the next generation nuclear reactors. Here, we report the irradiation responses of a novel multi-component alloy system, high entropy alloy (HEA) Al x CoCrFeNi ( x = 0.1, 0.75 and 1.5), focusing on their precipitation behavior. It is found that the single phase system, Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi, exhibits a great phase stability against ion irradiation. No precipitate is observed even at the highest fluence. In contrast, numerous coherent precipitates are present in both multi-phase HEAs. Based on the irradiation-induced/enhanced precipitation theory, the excellent structural stability against precipitation of Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi is attributed to the high configurational entropy and low atomic diffusion, which reduces the thermodynamic driving force and kinetically restrains the formation of precipitate, respectively. The CALPHAD-based HTCs

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. decision.trend: Early work on AlxCoCrFeNi HEAs examined how single-phase versus multiphase structures respond to external stimuli (ion irradiation), revealing distinct precipitation and stability behaviors (PMC4999872). Subsequent studies introduced high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) treatments for Al0.7CoCrFeNi to enhance both strength and ductility via a hierarchically organized multiphase microstructure (PMC11087546). More recent efforts on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs probed aging effects at different temperatures (e.g., 600 °C vs. 750 °C) to investigate tempering-like embrittlement and recovery of ductility, underscoring the critical role of targeted thermal profiles in controlling phase formation (PMC12806431).
decision.unsolved: Despite identifying distinct phase transformation pathways and mechanical responses to specific temperatures and pressures, there is no systematic, predictive method for guiding Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni phase evolution across the wide parameter space of processing routes, time, temperature, and atmosphere. Researchers lack a robust, unifying approach to expedite the design of heat treatments or processing schedules that ensure targeted phase fractions and optimal mechanical properties without guesswork or extensive trial-and-error.
decision.lever: Develop an advanced thermodynamic and kinetic sampling framework—leveraging multi-phase free-energy models and microstructure evolution simulations—to explore the interplay of temperature, time, and existing multiphase equilibria in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
decision.why: Building on observations that phase formation (FCC, B2, A2) and corresponding mechanical responses depend strongly on heating, cooling, and pressure histories, a systematic free-energy-based sampling scheme would enable rational design of heat treatment (or HPHT-like) parameters for controlled phase evolution. This approach can unify insights from existing experiments and reduce reliance on trial-and-error.
